01.note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi asked Abaye to set a time to study with him. Abaye said his daytime study was taken and at night he had to irrigate his fields, so Rav Shimi offered to do the irrigating by day so they could study at night, and Abaye agreed. Rav Shimi told the owners of the upper fields that the lower fields drink first, and told the lower owners that the upper fields drink first; while they argued, he dammed the river and watered Abaye's fields. Abaye told him he had acted on two opposing opinions at once, and would not taste that year's produce.
01.why: The Gemara has just said that since the law follows neither Rav (lower fields first) nor Shmuel (upper fields first), whoever is stronger prevails. Rav Shimi plays the two opinions against each other, and Abaye rejects water gained that way.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: A student who wants to study with Abaye and offers to irrigate his fields in exchange.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The teacher whose fields are watered; he refuses to eat the crop that came from the trick.

terms.meaning: Two Sages who disagreed over which fields along a river get the water first: in this story, Rav's view is that the lower fields drink first and Shmuel's that the upper fields do.

02.note: The people of a place called Bei Harmakh dug a channel at the head of the Shanvata River to run its water around their fields, then let it back into the river further down. The owners of the upstream fields complained to Abaye that this was damaging their river. Abaye told them to dig a little deeper alongside, but they said that would dry out their pits. Abaye then told the people of Bei Harmakh to take themselves away from there.
02.why: It follows another story about Abaye and disputes over river water for irrigation, part of the Gemara's discussion of who has first rights to shared water.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the upstream field owners bring their complaint to.

03.note: Rav Kahana was walking to Huzal when he saw a man throwing sticks at a palm tree to knock down dates. Rav Kahana gathered some of the fallen dates and ate them. The man told him that he had thrown them down with his own hand, so they were his. Rav Kahana answered that he must be from the town of Rabbi Yoshiya, and applied to Rabbi Yoshiya the verse: "And a righteous man is the foundation of the world."
03.why: The mishna says that taking olives that fall from a tree a poor man is gleaning is robbery only by the Sages' rule for the sake of peace, but a Sage taught that once they were in his hand it is full robbery. The man's claim matches that teaching, and Rav Kahana credits his town's learning.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who eats dates a stranger knocked down, and accepts the man's claim that they were his.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: A great Sage of Huzal; Rav Kahana credits him for the townsman's knowledge of the law.

terms.meaning: A town; the translation describes it as the place of Rabbi Yoshiya and a center of Torah study.

04.note: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda were sitting when the Sage Geneiva passed by. One said they should stand for him because he was learned in Torah; the other asked whether they should stand for an argumentative man. Geneiva came over and greeted them twice: "Peace be upon you, kings." They asked how he knew Sages are called kings and why a king's greeting is doubled, and he gave a verse for each. When they invited him to eat, he quoted Rav's teaching that a person may not taste anything before feeding his animal.
04.why: The Gemara has been discussing Rav's rule that one does not double the greeting of peace to a gentile; Geneiva's doubled greeting to the Sages shows when doubling is proper and where it comes from.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: One of the two Sages Geneiva greets.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: One of the two Sages Geneiva greets.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: A Sage whom one of the pair calls a son of Torah and the other calls argumentative.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Geneiva quotes his teachings, which he reports in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The authority behind the teachings Geneiva quotes.

terms.meaning: Saying "peace" twice. Geneiva learns from a verse where David is greeted "peace, peace be to you" that a king is greeted this way.

05.note: A man sent a bill of divorce to his wife by an agent. The agent found her kneading dough and told her to take it; she said, "Let it be in your hand." Rav Nahman said that if the law follows Rabbi Hanina, he would rule the divorce valid, but Rava objected that the husband's agent had not finished his task, so the wife could not make him her agent. They sent the question to Rabbi Ami, who said the divorce was not valid, while Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba asked for time; when they asked him again he said the matter was as uncertain to him as to them.
05.why: The Gemara is debating whether a wife can appoint an agent to receive her bill of divorce from her husband's agent. The case is left unsettled, and the Gemara goes on to treat the woman as possibly married and possibly divorced.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Says he would rule the divorce valid if the law follows Rabbi Hanina.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Objects that the husband's agent never completed his task.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Rules that the divorce does not take effect.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Asked twice; finally says the question is as uncertain to him as to those asking.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: His view, that a wife can appoint such an agent, is the question in the case.

terms.meaning: The document (in Hebrew, a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. It can be delivered by an agent, and a wife can also appoint an agent to receive it.

06.note: A husband told witnesses to write a bill of divorce for his wife, whose name was Nefata, but they wrote Tefata by mistake. Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta ruled in Rav's name that the document was invalid because of the wrong name, but that the witnesses could not write a new one, since they had already carried out their task.
06.why: Rabba and then Rav Nahman go on to object to this ruling, debating when witnesses who wrote a bill of divorce have finished their agency and when they may write another.

people.name: Nefata
people.about: The woman being divorced; the witnesses wrote her name wrongly as Tefata.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta
people.about: Rules on the case in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The authority in whose name the ruling is given.

terms.meaning: The document (in Hebrew, a get) that ends a marriage; it must name the wife correctly.
Finished the job they were appointed to do, so their authority to act for the husband is over.

07.note: Geneiva was being led out in a neck chain to be executed. As he went, he said: "Give four hundred dinars to Rabbi Avina from my wine in Nehar Panya." Rabbi Zeira said that Rabbi Avina should lift his basket and go to his teacher Rav Huna, who taught that a man's bill of divorce has the same status as his gift.
07.why: The mishna says a man led out to execution who says "Write a bill of divorce for my wife" is understood to mean that it should also be given to her. Rabbi Zeira ties this to Geneiva's dying gift through Rav Huna's teaching that the two are treated alike.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: A man led out to be executed who leaves money to Rabbi Avina.

people.name: Rabbi Avina
people.about: The man Geneiva leaves the four hundred dinars to.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Says Rabbi Avina can collect the gift by relying on his teacher Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rabbi Avina's teacher, who compared a deathbed bill of divorce to a deathbed gift.

terms.meaning: A collar placed on a condemned man being taken out to be executed.
A silver coin.

08.note: A man walked into a synagogue and found a schoolteacher, the teacher's son, and another man sitting there. He told them, "Two of you should write a bill of divorce for my wife." The schoolteacher then died, and the question arose whether the son and the other man could write it. Rav Nahman said people do not appoint a son as agent in his father's place; Rav Pappi said they do; Rava ruled that they do.
08.why: The Gemara is discussing when a husband's spoken instruction to write a bill of divorce is enough to act on; this case asks who exactly he appointed when he said "two of you."

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Holds that the son cannot step in for his father.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Holds that the son can step in for his father.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that the son can step in.

terms.meaning: Someone appointed to act for another person, here to write and deliver a bill of divorce. A father and son cannot serve together as witnesses because they are relatives.

09.note: Shmuel reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled the law follows Rabbi Yosei, who says spoken instructions cannot be handed on to an agent. His son, Rabbi Shimon, asked why, since Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Hanina of Ono disagree with Rabbi Yosei. His father told him: "Be silent, my son, be silent. You did not see Rabbi Yosei; if you had, you would know that his reasoning goes with his statements."
09.why: The Gemara has been working out where Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei on passing a husband's instructions to another agent; this exchange gives the ruling Shmuel relies on, and a baraita follows describing Rabbi Yosei and other Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rules the law follows Rabbi Yosei and defends it to his son.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who questions the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage whose opinion is accepted; his reasoning goes with his statements.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Reports Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Disagrees with Rabbi Yosei, along with Rabbi Hanina of Ono.

terms.meaning: An instruction someone only spoke (such as a husband telling people to write a bill of divorce) cannot be passed on by them to a further agent.

10.note: The members of the Exilarch's house would torment Rav Amram the pious by making him lie all night on the snow. The next day they would ask what he wanted to eat. Knowing they would do the opposite of whatever he said, he asked for red meat roasted over coals and diluted wine, and they brought him fatty meat and undiluted wine, which is what he wanted. Yalta, Rav Nahman's wife, heard about it and took him to the bathhouse, keeping him in the water until it turned red like blood and his flesh was covered with coin-like spots.
10.why: The Gemara has just given remedies: red roasted meat with diluted wine for fever, fatty roasted meat with undiluted wine for chills. Rav Amram uses that very knowledge to get the cure for chills.

people.name: Rav Amram the pious
people.about: A Sage tormented by the Exilarch's household.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Nahman's wife, who takes Rav Amram to the bathhouse.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia; his household and servants appear here.

11.note: The Exilarch asked Rav Sheshet, who was blind, why he would not eat with him. Rav Sheshet said the servants were suspected of eating flesh cut from a living animal, and proved it: his servant stole a leg from a slaughtered animal, the servants then brought three legs, cut a leg from a living animal to make four, and the stolen one made five. At the meal the servants hid a small bone in his meat to choke him, so he wrapped the meat in his scarf; they then claimed a silver cup was stolen, found the meat, and said he wanted only to shame them, but he said it had a leprous spot, and on checking it did. As he left they covered a pit with a mat; Rav Hisda snorted to warn him, a child recited "Turn to your right or to your left," and he went around it.
11.why: It continues the Gemara's run of stories about Sages and the house of the Exilarch, following the story of Rav Amram, whom the Exilarch's household tormented.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A blind Sage who will not eat at the Exilarch's table and sees through the servants' tricks.

people.name: Exilarch
people.about: The leader whose servants Rav Sheshet suspects.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Present at the end; snorts to warn Rav Sheshet of the pit and asks how he knew.

terms.meaning: Flesh cut from an animal while it is still alive, which Jewish law forbids eating.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
Rav Sheshet quotes Rav Hisda that black spots on white skin or white spots on black skin are a sign of disease in the animal.

12.note: A remedy for intestinal pain is to take three hundred long peppers and drink a hundred of them in wine each day. Ravin of Neresh prepared a hundred and fifty of the local peppers in this way for the daughter of Rav Ashi, and she was healed.
12.why: It comes in a long list of remedies the Gemara gives for illnesses; this one carries a report of it being used.

people.name: Ravin of Neresh
people.about: Prepares the pepper remedy for Rav Ashi's daughter.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: His daughter is healed by the remedy.

13.note: For an illness of the spleen, one remedy is to roast a fish in a blacksmith's shop, eat it with the water used there to cool the hot metal, and drink that water. As evidence, the Gemara tells of a goat that used to drink water at a blacksmith's shop; when it was slaughtered, no spleen was found inside it.
13.why: It comes in the Gemara's list of remedies for an illness of the spleen, as evidence that the blacksmith's water works.

14.note: A remedy for a skin disease called lichen is to roast seven large wheat kernels on the blade of a new hoe, extract their oil and rub it on the skin. Rav Shimi bar Ashi used this remedy on a gentile who had "something else," which the translation explains as leprosy, and he was healed.
14.why: It comes in a long list of remedies the Gemara gives for illnesses; this one carries a report of it being used.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Uses the remedy to heal a gentile.

15.note: Abaye said that someone who does the six exhausting acts just listed in that order dies, and someone who does them out of order becomes weak. The Gemara objects that a woman named Me'oret made her slave do three of them and he died. The Gemara answers that that slave was weak.
15.why: The Gemara has just listed six acts that kill a person if done one after another; Me'oret's slave is brought as a challenge to Abaye's claim that doing them out of order only weakens him.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Says the six acts kill only when done in order.

people.name: Me'oret
people.about: A woman who made her slave perform three of the acts.

16.note: When Rabba bar Avuh was ill, Rav Huna and Rav Nahman went to visit him. Rav Huna told Rav Nahman to ask him whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei; Rav Nahman said he did not even know Rabbi Yosei's reason, and Rav Huna promised to tell him afterward. Rabba bar Avuh answered in Rav's name that the law does follow Rabbi Yosei. After they left, Rav Huna explained Rabbi Yosei's reason: the date written in a document proves when it takes effect.
16.why: The Gemara is asking whether Rav Huna was uncertain about following Rabbi Yosei. This visit shows he accepted Rabbi Yosei's view, so the Gemara concludes he was unsure only whether it applies when the husband adds a spoken condition.

people.name: Rabba bar Avuh
people.about: An ill Sage asked for the ruling; he answers in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Wants the ruling and explains Rabbi Yosei's reason afterward.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Asks the question at Rav Huna's request.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage whose opinion is in question.

terms.term: The date of a document proves
terms.meaning: Rabbi Yosei's principle that the date written on a document shows it takes effect from that day, even if this is not stated explicitly.

17.note: A man sold land and took on responsibility for any accident that might happen to it; then a river was diverted through it. The buyer came before Ravina, who told the seller to pay, but Rav Aha bar Tahalifa said this was an uncommon accident. The case reached Rava, who agreed it was uncommon. Ravina raised a teaching about a bill of divorce against him, Rava answered that the same teaching points the other way in its first clause, and in the end Ravina told Rav Aha of Difti that the teaching was corrupt and one must follow reason.
17.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching on a bill of divorce conditioned on dying of an illness, where the house collapsed or a snake bit. This sale case tests whether such a condition covers rare accidents, using that same teaching.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: First rules the seller must pay, later accepts that a rare accident is not covered.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Tahalifa
people.about: Objects that a river diverted through land is an uncommon accident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules it an uncommon accident and answers Ravina's objection.

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: Asks Ravina whether the teaching can still be used as an objection.

terms.meaning: Damage or loss no one could prevent. The question is whether a promise to cover "any accident" includes rare ones.
A teaching from the time of the mishna that was not included in the mishna itself.

18.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, bought sesame on the bank of the Malka River and hired sailors to carry it across, who took on responsibility for any accident. Then the river was dammed. The two Sages told the sailors to hire donkeys and bring the sesame, but when they came before Rava he called them "white geese who strip people of their cloaks" and said this was an uncommon accident.
18.why: The Gemara has just concluded that a promise to cover any accident does not include rare ones; this case applies that conclusion.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: One of the two Sages who bought the sesame.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Rav Pappa's partner in buying the sesame.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, who rules against the two Sages.

terms.meaning: Rava's insult for the two Sages; the translation says it refers to their long white beards.

19.note: A landowner told his sharecropper: everyone else waters a field three times and takes a quarter of the crop; you water it four times and take a third. In the end rain fell, so the fourth watering was not needed. Rav Yosef said he did not water a fourth time, so he gets only a quarter; Rabba said the fourth watering was not needed, so he gets a third.
19.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a condition must be carried out exactly or only in its purpose, as with a bill of divorce given on a condition. It asks whether Rav Yosef and Rabba follow the two sides of that dispute, and concludes that both follow the Rabbis.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Rules the sharecropper gets only a quarter.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rules the sharecropper gets a third.

terms.meaning: A farmer who works another person's field in return for a share of the crop.

20.note: A teaching reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: "After the Festival" means thirty days after it. Rabbi Hiyya went out and taught this in public in his name, and the people praised it; when he taught it as the view of the majority, they did not praise it.
20.why: The Gemara is working out how long time phrases like "after a year" or "after a week" mean in a conditional bill of divorce. It concludes from the reaction that the law does not follow this view.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The Sage who taught that after the Festival means thirty days.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Teaches the ruling in public, first in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's name and then as the majority view.

terms.meaning: One of the pilgrimage festivals of the Jewish year.
